picked.t: How Australia's tighter visa rules might affect international students' study and migration pathways
picked.body: Hong Hai, from Hai Phong, arrived in Australia last year on a 462 visa, which allows holders to work and travel. After doing some research, he learned that Tasmania offered relatively favorable policies for international students and faced worker shortages. He planned to pursue vocational training, find a job and eventually seek permanent residency. While Hai was researching how to apply for a student visa (subclass 500), the Australian government announced a series of tighter policies affecting foreigners. As announced by the Australian government, starting Oct. 2, international students will only be allowed to progress to higher levels of study, rather than repeatedly enrolling in courses at the same or a lower level, under Australia's student visa (subclass 500) rules. Most foreigners and international students in Australia can no longer apply for a student visa from within the country. According to Australia's Department of Home Affairs, students seeking this type of visa must now apply and wait for a decision from outside Australia. The department late last month also announced that Australia will stop foreign students from bringing partners and children to accompany them while they study, with certain exemptions for students from ASEAN and Pacific nations, and those taking PhD courses. After seeing the high student visa refusal rate, Hai became uncertain about whether he should apply for another Australian visa. If rejected, he would not only lose his application fee but also have the refusal recorded in his immigration history, potentially creating obstacles when applying for visas in some other countries. Australian Department of Home Affairs data show that the student visa refusal rate reached 24.2% in June 2026, meaning roughly one in four applications was refused. ABC reported that this was the highest refusal rate in a decade, up from 7.9% in June 2016. "I feel that policies are becoming increasingly difficult for immigrants, especially international students," Hai said. Over the past three years, the Australian government has taken various measures to control net migration as inflation has pushed up housing and other living costs. International students, who account for about one-third of temporary visa holders, have become a key target of these efforts. Since 2024, Australia has raised student visa fees three times, shortened the post-study work period for international graduates and increased financial proof requirements, among other measures. Shortly before announcing the latest regulations, the government last month barred a postgraduate course that was reportedly being used by some international students as a pathway to permanent residency. Genuine students face fewer roadblocks Experts say the new policies will have a greater impact on people who study primarily to extend their legal stay and pursue migration pathways than on those with genuine study goals and clear plans. "A strategy that is primarily based on securing a visa first and then finding a way to stay and migrate will become more uncertain," said Professor Ly Tran Thi of Deakin University. She said Vietnamese students, as nationals of an ASEAN country, as well as PhD students, will still be allowed to bring family members to Australia under the new rules. This provides a degree of stability for them and their families. Nguyen Duc Quyet, CEO and co-founder of education and migration consultancy Rightway, added that applicants for Master by Research programs may also be allowed to bring family members, as these programs could fall under the category of "postgraduate research programs." However, he said this needs to be confirmed by official regulations. Based on individual states' workforce attraction strategies and the government's latest direction, migration opportunities are increasingly concentrated in five groups of occupations, according to Nguyen Duy Tung, an Australian migration representative at Rightway Education & Services, a consultancy specializing in Australian study, migration and skills assessment, with offices in Melbourne, Adelaide and Ho Chi Minh City. They include construction and infrastructure; healthcare and health services; education and teaching; agriculture, fisheries and resources; and security, defense and policing, he said. Skilled visas such as subclasses 491, 190 and 494, which are commonly pursued after subclass 500 or 485 visas, remain a priority in regional areas. These areas are outside major cities such as Sydney, Melbourne and Brisbane. Students can receive an additional one to two years on their 485 visas in regional areas, giving them more time to gain work experience and accumulate points for migration. However, Professor Ly cautioned international students against assuming that studying a particular field will guarantee a pathway to permanent residency, as labor market demand changes over time and migration policies change accordingly. picked.t: Da Nang accommodation options cater to different travel needs
picked.body: For some visitors, a Da Nang trip starts with an early walk along My Khe Beach. Others prioritize food, sightseeing or time with family. The best accommodation therefore depends less on the number of facilities or the lowest advertised rate than on three factors: group size, length of stay and how much time guests expect to spend at the property. Location and hotels for shorter stays Travelers should first choose an area based on their itinerary before comparing accommodation. Those planning to swim or walk along the shore may prefer My Khe Beach, while visitors focused on the Museum of Cham Sculpture, city dining and walks along Bach Dang Street may find the central area more convenient. For mixed itineraries, comparing travel times to frequently visited places can help identify the most practical location. Everyday convenience, such as easy access to breakfast or a quick trip back with tired children, may matter more than proximity to a single attraction. For couples, solo travelers and small families on short visits, a beachfront hotel can make the coast part of the daily routine while providing services such as breakfast, housekeeping and reception support. A comfortable room may be sufficient for guests who spend most of their time exploring the city. Before booking, travelers should check the property's exact location and beach access, bed arrangements and included services. Apartments when daily routines matter For longer stays, a kitchen, laundry facilities and a separate workspace can be more useful than hotel services. Self-catering apartments can suit families with young children, remote workers and travelers who prefer to prepare some meals themselves. Layouts vary from studios with kitchenettes to larger units with separate bedrooms, living areas and full kitchens. Travelers should check the appliances and cooking equipment provided, laundry arrangements and cleaning schedules. For extended stays, they should also confirm whether electricity, water and other charges are included. Remote workers should verify the availability of a suitable workspace and reliable internet connection rather than relying solely on a general Wi-Fi listing. Whole-house villas for larger groups For larger families or groups of friends, an entire villa can provide shared living space while allowing guests to stay under one roof. Hanami Villa Da Nang at 276/7 Ngu Hanh Son Street is one example. According to its operator, the property is rented as a whole and has six bedrooms, shared living areas, a private pool, two kitchens, a cinema room, a steam room and a rooftop area. The operator says it can accommodate up to 16 guests. The villa is in a residential area rather than directly on the beachfront. It is managed by Nami Stay , which provides local support during guests' stays. For larger rentals, travelers should check the floor plan, bed allocation, stairs and bathroom access, particularly when traveling with people with limited mobility. Families should also ask about pool safety and other measures before arrival. Price comparisons should cover the full stay rather than the advertised nightly rate alone. Travelers should compare the same dates and group size while checking taxes, mandatory fees, deposits, cleaning or utility charges, cancellation terms and extra-person fees. For villas, they should also confirm whether the booking provides exclusive use of the property. Weather is another consideration. When rain disrupts outdoor plans, indoor communal space can become particularly useful for families and groups. Ultimately, a beachfront hotel can suit shorter stays centered on sightseeing and the coast, an apartment can support longer-term daily routines, while a whole-house villa can give larger groups more shared space. The best choice is the one whose location, layout, services and booking terms match the travelers and their plans, rather than simply the property that looks most appealing in photographs.

picked.t: Vietnamese trainees face debt, exploitation in Europe's largest economy despite promise of free training
picked.body: In late August, Hong Hanh, 23, attended a conciliation hearing with her former employer at the Berlin Chamber of Commerce and Industry (IHK Berlin) to contest what she says was an unlawful dismissal. The Ho Chi Minh City native had spent nine months in Germany, shocked by her meager take-home pay and constant work. When exhaustion forced her to ask for sick leave, she said, her broker and the restaurant owner pressed her to sign a voluntary resignation that would strip her of unemployment benefits. She refused and was immediately handed a dismissal notice. The restaurant owner did not attend the hearing, sending a lawyer who argued the dismissal was valid because Hanh had shown no interest in the job. With no agreement reached, her industry's trade union is providing legal support to take the case to the Labor Court, which is expected to hear it late this year. "When I came to Germany for vocational training, I could not have imagined going through these difficulties," Hanh said. Germany is Europe's largest economy and the world's third largest, behind the U.S. and China, according to International Monetary Fund data. Vocational training in Germany took off among Vietnamese around 2018-2019 as the country eased its rules, including through the Skilled Immigration Act, to address labor shortages. The biggest draw is the dual "Ausbildung" model, under which trainees pay no tuition and receive a monthly training wage. Some Vietnamese brokers went on to market it as a route to a better life. About 16,000 young Vietnamese are now in vocational training in Germany, according to the Federal Employment Agency. Germany's Migration Report 2024 says Vietnamese made up 21% of foreign nationals who entered the country for vocational training. Income shock Hanh learned of the route from a friend while in her second year of university and dropped out to study German. In late 2025, after paying €7,000 (US$7,900) in broker fees, she arrived in Berlin. She worked at a local restaurant while waiting for her course to formally begin, and realized the high income the broker had advertised blurred gross pay (Brutto) with take-home pay (Netto). Her contract set gross pay at €1,068 a month, but she took home only €787, half of which went on rent. Although her payslip listed a "meal allowance," she still paid €68 a month out of pocket to eat at work. "I have to budget every cent of the little that is left," she said. To survive in a city as expensive as Berlin, many trainees in her position share rooms without a formal rental contract. With no name on a mailbox, they miss important letters from the authorities and insurers. Short of money, some work off the books in restaurants for less than the minimum wage, with no contract and no days off. They know they are being exploited but put up with it because of living costs and debts back home. Under German rules, recruitment fees are paid by the hiring employer. But a study published in August 2025 by the Berlin-based Minor institute found that 57% of Vietnamese trainees came to Germany through private brokers, paying fees of €6,000-15,000 ($6,750-16,900). A 2024 study by Freie Universität Berlin and reports by public broadcaster ARD estimated the figure could reach €20,000-40,000 ($22,500-45,000). Many families who spend tens of thousands of euros believe their children are securing a stable future in Europe. At an elderly care provider in Altenburg, in the state of Thuringia, a scandal broke in early 2026. The provider had lost its training license in August 2025 but concealed the fact, making 27 Vietnamese nursing trainees work unpaid for four to eight months while living in containers. In mid-January 2026, when the trainees went on strike to demand their rights, they were evicted from their accommodation in the snow. "By the time they called for help, they had lost everything: housing, their training place, their jobs and their income," Michael Tirp, director of VDP Personal Bildung Integration, which runs an emergency SOS hotline for Vietnamese workers in Germany, told VnExpress . The organization immediately launched a fundraising drive to arrange temporary housing for the group. Phuong Nga, 24, from the outskirts of Hanoi, was among them. Unpaid for half a year and left without a training place, she sheltered at a nail salon on money sent by her family. Tirp said that within a month the organization had helped her sign a contract with a new employer and find her own apartment. Hanh also described being exploited. German labor law requires a break of at least 30 minutes on shifts of six to nine hours, but she said the restaurant's timekeeping system always showed her working eight hours with a break and erased all overtime records. Worn out, she fell ill and was fired. "The broker told me to just sign the resignation and they would find me another place. picked.t: Why are Korean visitors to Vietnam declining?
picked.body: Vietnam welcomed 17.7 million international visitors in the first nine months, up almost 15% year-on-year, the General Statistics Office reported. South Korea ranked second, after mainland China, with 3 million arrivals, but was the only top-10 market to record a decline, down about 5%. Korean arrivals also fell 5% in 2025, when total arrivals hit a record of more than 21 million. South Koreans made over 19 million overseas trips in the first eight months, up 2%, according to the Korea Tourism Organization. Martin Koerner, commercial director of Anam Group, which manages two resorts in Mui Ne and Cam Ranh, says Korean demand is still growing but shifting elsewhere. Yanolja Research found that only three of the 12 most-visited destinations for Koreans grew in the first half. Japan rose 18.6% to 5.6 million visits, 40% of Korean outbound travelers. Mainland China rose 16%, while Macau grew 0.7%. The other nine destinations, mostly in Southeast Asia and the U.S., all declined. Vietnam fell more than 2%, and Thailand dropped the most, at 24%. Pham Hai Quynh, director of the Asia Tourism Development Institute, attributes the decline partly to growing competition from China and Japan. Quynh says Japan offers a good exchange rate, easy transport and quality service. China has attractive tour prices, visa-free entry for Koreans since late 2025 and more direct flights. A weak won is a factor. The currency fell to 1,536 won per U.S. dollar on June 3, its lowest since 2009, and now sits around 1,350. Korea JoongAng Daily reports that the weak currency is changing how South Koreans travel. They are shopping less, opting for Airbnb-style rentals over luxury hotels. Hanatour, one of South Korea's largest travel companies, says Korean travelers used to favor cheap tours with shopping stops. Now they choose pricier packages without shopping to cut down on extra spending. However, travel spending in Japan continues to rise, as the weak yen makes the destination more affordable. In 2025, South Korean visitors spent a record $5.7 billion in Japan. Koerner adds that beyond cost, the convenience of the trip also shapes Korean choices. A flight of two to three hours to Japan or China beats a six-hour trip to Southeast Asia. "In this context, Vietnam's edge as a low-cost destination no longer creates a big enough gap to hold on to Korean visitors," Quynh says. Saturation is another problem. Quynh says a destination's life cycle lasts three to four years, after which travelers seek something new. Da Nang, Nha Trang and Phu Quoc have been promoted in Korea since around 2023, and golf and spa packages have grown familiar. Fewer flights have hurt too. Higher fuel prices from the Middle East conflict led Korean airlines, mainly low-cost carriers, to cut 1,000 flights between April and June. Yanolja Research also says Vietnam's image has been linked to Cambodian scam compounds. Negative sentiment toward Vietnam once reached 18%. To win Koreans back, Quynh says Vietnam should refresh its image, rely less on cheap beach holidays, and develop cultural, ecological and wellness products. He also urges more promotion in Busan, Daegu and Gwangju cities. According to ET News , Vietnam remains the most popular Southeast Asian destination among South Koreans. Koerner says Vietnam needs to offer new experiences to bring back Korean travelers, many of whom have already visited the country. He states destinations, airlines, hotels, travel companies and online travel agencies should work together on packages with competitive prices and appealing experiences. Promotions also need to come sooner, as Korean travelers book just weeks before departure rather than months ahead. "The most important question is how Vietnam can beat its rivals and become the top choice at the moment travelers decide to book," he says.

picked.t: Hundreds queue from dawn in overloaded Ho Chi Minh City cancer hospital
picked.body: At around 5 a.m. on Oct. 6, the second branch of Ho Chi Minh City Oncology Hospital in Thu Duc is already packed, with long lines of people waiting to get queue tokens to see the doctor. The hospital has chairs, but there were not enough for all the visitors. The facility receives 4,800 to 5,000 people every day, including about 700 for radiotherapy, with most coming from provinces and cities across the country. The hospital has 10 radiotherapy machines working in three shifts, from 5 a.m. to 11 p.m. every day. For the machines to deliver their first radiation treatment at 5 a.m., technical staff must arrive between 3 and 4 a.m. to perform checks, measurements, and quality assurance procedures. The radiotherapy department opens at 5 a.m., but half an hour earlier their seating areas and corridors are already crowded with patients waiting for treatment. According to Dr. Diep Bao Tuan, director of the Ho Chi Minh City Oncology Hospital, the 10 radiotherapy machines are running at full capacity and treating about 700 patients a day, but another 800-1,000 people remain on the waiting list. Patients wait an average of four to six weeks for their turn. According to Dr. Diep Bao Tuan, director of the Ho Chi Minh City Oncology Hospital, the 10 radiotherapy machines are running at full capacity and treating about 700 patients a day, but another 800-1,000 people remain on the waiting list. Patients wait an average of four to six weeks for their turn. Each patient waits for about an hour for their radiotherapy session. Many, exhausted, sleep on benches along the corridors. To cut the time needed to change equipment and accessories between sessions, the hospital often schedules patients with similar conditions consecutively. These are among the measures being used while the hospital waits for additional capacity. Bong, a 63-year-old woman from An Giang, came to Ho Chi Minh City for treatment for endometrial cancer. After surgery in June, she waited for a month and a half before beginning radiotherapy. She chose the first session of the day at 5 a.m. so that she could finish early and return to her rented room to rest. She is now on her 21st out of 28 sessions. For the treatment, she has paid an advance of VND10 million (US$385) after the amount covered by health insurance was deducted. A 59-year-old man from Gia Lai in the Central Highlands sat waiting in a corner of the department corridor from early morning. He had surgery for a meningioma a year earlier but did not undergo the recommended radiotherapy because he believed the tumor was benign. When the disease recurred, he had to undergo a second operation followed by radiotherapy. After surgery, he waited for more than two months to begin radiotherapy. "At first, the doctor said I would have to wait six weeks, but it ended up being eight," he said. " I was worried because the disease had already come back once, but with so many patients, there was nothing else I could do." Radiotherapy is not the only service under pressure; Other areas are also crowded from before dawn. The overload is expected to ease somewhat since Ho Chi Minh City recently approved more than VND5 trillion (US$192.5 million) to expand the hospital in 2026-2030. The expansion will include a new high-tech disease screening center, purchases of specialized medical equipment including a cyclotron system and single-energy linear accelerator, a new proton therapy center, and a new support facility for patients. The city is also developing a multi-tier healthcare network, including the Oncology Hospital's Ba Ria and Binh Duong campuses and medical clusters in Tan Kien and Thu Duc, in an effort to expand cancer treatment capacity and reduce pressure on existing facilities. picked.t: Casting nets: floodwaters bring seasonal bounty to Vietnam's Mekong Delta
picked.body: The annual flood season is a natural cycle in the Mekong Delta, typically lasting from August to November. As water from the Mekong River and upstream areas flows into the region, vast areas of farmland become submerged. While the flooding can disrupt daily life and agriculture, it also replenishes nutrients in the soil and creates favorable conditions for fish, shrimp and other aquatic species to thrive, providing local communities with an important seasonal source of food and income. The annual floods also help clean the fields, eliminate weeds and pests, and deposit nutrient-rich alluvial soil. In this photo taken in Dong Thap Province, residents take their fishing gear into the fields to catch local specialties such as cyprinid fish, shrimp, crabs and eels, as the floodwaters arrive. After more than 30 years of making a living by setting fishing traps, Le Van Son, from Thuong Lac Commune, Dong Thap, said his income depends on how high the water rises. Only when the water spreads across the fields and remains there for an extended period does it bring in large quantities of shrimp and fish. "This job is enough to get us through a few months of the flood season, but it does not leave us with much extra," he said. Flying minnow, a small fish familiar to Mekong Delta residents, appears in large numbers during the flood season. The fish grows to only about the size of a finger, has tender meat and is commonly braised with pepper, deep-fried or cooked in soup. During the flood season, it is relatively cheap, selling for VND10,000-15,000 (US$0.38-0.58) per kilogram fresh, while dead fish sold as bait for larger fish can cost just a few thousand dong. Brothers in An Hoa Commune, Dong Thap, head into the inundated field carrying nets to set fish traps. A flood level of roughly half a meter creates optimal working conditions, reducing the physical strain of wading through deep water while extending the window to harvest seasonal aquatic specialties. Flood-season catches provide the essential raw materials powering Hong Ngu Ward's traditional dried freshwater fish craft village in Dong Thap. Home to roughly 20 households engaged in the production, the village is renowned for its dried snakehead, gourami, and catfish. People clean, butterfly, salt, and season the fresh catch before laying the fish out to dry under the sun, a time-tested process that locks in their natural sweetness. Wet markets swell with an influx of freshwater crabs and fish during the flood season, with supplies driving prices lower than in the dry months. At Hong Ngu Market, crab vendor Duong Thi Huynh Nhu purchases hundreds of kilograms of crabs daily to keep up with brisk demand. Nhu sells large crab claws separately for VND280,000 to VND300,000 per kilogram, while the remaining meat is finely ground to prepare rieu , a traditional Vietnamese crab soup base. "The flood season is such a good time to sell," Nhu noted. picked.t: 9 Asian cities food lovers shouldn't miss in 2026, including Ho Chi Minh City
picked.body: The list highlights how local ingredients, generations of cooking traditions, and modern kitchens make each destination worth a food-focused trip. HCMC is Vietnam's only representative, joining Seoul, Taipei, Hong Kong, Manila, Singapore, Penang, Bangkok and Tokyo. Ho Chi Minh City, Vietnam Street food is a major draw in HCMC, where bowls of pho and neighborhood coffee shops offer a taste of everyday life. Young chefs are giving familiar Vietnamese ingredients fresh expression, building seasonal menus that connect contemporary cooking with the flavors of everyday meals. Michelin highlighted CieL, a restaurant taking a modern approach to Vietnamese ingredients, and ST25 by KOTO, named after the Vietnamese rice variety that features in several of its dishes. Together, they illustrate the city's growing culinary range: visitors can explore local flavors at street level, then discover how chefs develop those same foundations in a restaurant setting. Seoul, South Korea Seoul rewards an appetite for specialties. Many of its most characteristic restaurants concentrate on a single dish, whether a clear, deeply flavored beef broth or raw crab steeped in marinade. Fermented pastes and sauces give much of the city's cooking its distinctive depth. Those flavors also underpin contemporary Korean dining. At Mingles, a three-Michelin-starred restaurant, traditional ingredients are woven into modern tasting menus. From a neighborhood soup house to an ambitious dining room, Seoul offers different ways to discover the care and complexity behind Korean cooking. Taipei, Taiwan Beef noodles, braised pork rice, and steamed buns filled with meat provide an inviting introduction to Taipei. These everyday favorites also help shape the city's contemporary restaurants, where the flavors of street stalls and night markets remain important reference points. Taipei's chefs bring a local accent to international cooking. At Eika, a contemporary Japanese restaurant, fermented tofu and soy milk find their way into carefully composed menus. For travelers, moving between night markets and restaurants reveals how Taiwanese ingredients and tastes give imported cuisines a character of their own. Hong Kong Roast goose, wonton noodles, char siu barbecued pork, and dim sum remain central to Hong Kong's food culture. Busy noodle shops and lively dining halls offer some of the most direct ways to experience it. The city's appeal also lies in its breadth. Restaurants serving the regional cuisines of Ningbo, Shanghai, and Shunde sit alongside an international dining scene. Amber, a three-Michelin-starred French restaurant known for dairy-free cooking, represents another direction. Visitors can explore both longstanding Chinese traditions and contemporary experimentation. Manila, Philippines In Manila, family recipes and regional traditions are giving chefs a rich foundation for contemporary cooking. Michelin highlighted slowly simmered broths, carefully judged sourness and familiar flavors, with technique supporting the food rather than dominating it. Linamnam, an intimate restaurant with just 10 covers, reflects that approach through dishes rooted in the chef's memories and local traditions. Beyond individual restaurants, shared plates and leisurely meals are part of the attraction. Exploring a neighborhood over several meals offers visitors a taste of both Filipino cooking and the social life surrounding it. Singapore Singapore's hawker stalls and fine-dining restaurants draw inspiration from one another. Michelin noted that techniques once associated with elaborate tasting menus are appearing in modest stalls, while restaurant chefs increasingly turn to familiar local flavors. Travelers can begin with noodles at a hawker center, a collection of food stalls, before exploring contemporary cooking at Seroja, a restaurant inspired by the culinary traditions of the Malay Archipelago. Across different budgets and settings, this exchange gives visitors a way to taste the city's multicultural identity. Penang, Malaysia Penang's food culture is rooted in dishes such as wok-fried flat rice noodles, tangy fish-based noodle soup, and rice served with an assortment of curries. These street-food staples reflect the island's mix of communities and remain central to everyday eating. Contemporary restaurants draw on that same heritage. In George Town, Penang's capital, restored buildings provide distinctive settings for new dining experiences. Au Jardin, a restaurant in a former bus depot, combines French technique with local flavors. Eating at both street stalls and modern restaurants reveals different expressions of the island's culinary traditions. Bangkok, Thailand Bangkok's chefs are looking more closely at Thailand's regional recipes and seasonal produce. Menus increasingly identify farmers and ingredient origins, giving diners a clearer sense of where their food comes from. picked.t: Vietnam must ensure tax policy stability to retain and attract foreign investors: officials
picked.body: Investors demand predictability Vietnam's foreign direct investment (FDI) strategy is entering a new phase after nearly four decades of courting overseas capital. The earlier task was to make the environment attractive enough to draw international cash. The tougher challenge now is keeping quality capital, getting investors to expand and extracting more value for the economy. With competition for FDI intensifying, multinationals weigh more than their tax bills. They also look at compliance costs, the risk of policy shifts, how rules are enforced and how long it takes to solve new problems. A clear, stable and predictable tax policy has become a core part of investment competitiveness. Mai Xuan Thanh, Director of the Taxation Department, said companies also want to know whether policies are clear, obligations predictable and rules enforced consistently, and whether proper channels exist for dialogue and problem-solving when issues arise. The demand is sharpest for foreign-invested firms, whose production and trade often span multiple markets, entities and tax systems. Related-party transactions, double taxation avoidance agreements, advance pricing agreements, information exchange and data transparency can directly affect costs and planning. From tax incentives to long-term investment climate Nguyen Anh Tuan, Deputy Director of the Foreign Investment Agency under the Ministry of Finance (MoF), said the goal is no longer simply to raise capital volumes or project counts. Authorities want better quality, efficiency and sustainability in capital flows, and closer links between the FDI sector, domestic capabilities and long-term development goals. That shift is set out in the Politburo's Resolution 10-NQ/TW dated June 8, 2026 on developing the foreign-invested sector. It calls for moving from scale and quantity toward quality, efficiency and added value, and prioritises projects with advanced technologies, modern governance and innovation capacity that can plug deeper into global value chains. Roux Eloïse, a representative of the European Union Delegation to Vietnam, said predictability is key for countries seeking to attract and keep foreign companies. Vietnam holds considerable advantages in its domestic market, infrastructure, logistics and network of free trade agreements, but a transparent, stable legal and tax environment will unlock more room for investment cooperation. On Sept. 22, 2026, the government issued the Resolution 280/NQ-CP on an action plan to realize the Resolution 10-NQ/TW that assigns 61 tasks to ministries, agencies and localities. The MoF was assigned 22 key tasks covering direct and indirect investment and capital market development. Tighter coordination among investment, tax and customs authorities is central, both to ease business operations and ensure policies are enforced as intended. Alongside improved investment legislation, tax administration should rest on data and risk management, so firms can comply proactively. Thanh stressed that "transparency is a requirement for both sides". Companies must ensure records and data truthfully reflect the substance of transactions and engage in dialogue early when complex issues arise. Tax authorities, in turn, need to publish policies, give clear guidance, enforce rules consistently and deliver information in a timely manner.

picked.t: Residents wade through half-meter floodwaters as year's highest tide swamps Ho Chi Minh City streets
picked.body: At around 4 p.m., a tide of more than 1.7 m, the highest in HCMC this year, leaves Pham Huu Lau Street in the former District 7 in the city's southern area under half a meter of water along a stretch of about 3 km. picked.t: Southeast Asian capital sees travel interest spike for Eurovision Asia Grand Final
picked.body: Vietnam recorded the region's strongest growth, with travel interest surging 105% from 2025, according to online travel platform Agoda. India ranked second with a 43% increase, highlighting continued demand among Indian travelers for short-haul trips to Southeast Asia. Malaysia saw a more modest 4% rise, building on its established travel ties with Thailand. The contest marks a milestone for the region: the first-ever pan-Asian expansion of the 70-year-old Eurovision franchise, bringing finalists from 11 countries to the stage for a potential regional audience of millions. Visitors heading to Bangkok for the Grand Final can choose from four neighborhoods, each offering a different experience. Siam is ideal for shopping and easy transport connections, with major malls, boutiques and cultural attractions. Thonglor and Ekkamai cater to nightlife lovers with cocktail bars, live music venues and popular restaurants, Agoda recommended. Sathorn offers upscale hotels, fine dining and rooftop bars with skyline and river views. For a taste of Thai heritage, Bangkok's Old Town features landmarks such as the Grand Palace, Wat Pho and Wat Arun, alongside traditional canals and historic streets. Thailand's capital Bangkok has been named the world's best city in this year's Readers' Choice Awards by British travel magazine Condé Nast Traveller.
